newsitem.title: UK: Bull markets, low inflation -- can it last?
newsitem.headline: Bull markets, low inflation -- can it last?

text.p: Persistently low inflation in the world's major economies has added gusto to a blistering rally in stock and bond markets.
Records have been smashed in New York and London, partly thanks to a return to the 1960s dream-team of sound growth and low inflation in the U.S. and Britain.

"There's almost this idyllic scenario for asset markets of no real inflationary pressures and budget deficits still being ratcheted down as income tax receipts come in," said Bank America senior economic adviser Jeremy Hawkins in London.
But can the good times last?
Is the return to stable prices just the luck of the economic cycle, or has government pre-occupation with stifling inflation sparked a new, improved, low inflation era?
"You can never say that inflation is completely dead, but if authorities act in a certain way, you can say it's dormant for a very long time," said Philip Shaw, economist at Investec Bank.
Low inflation was still at the top of government agendas, he said, and with a growing number of central banks turning independent over the years, price rises would continue to be muzzled.
With this in mind, markets are gradually becoming convinced subdued inflation is here to stay.
That confidence helped blast the U.S. stock market to new heights on Wednesday as the Dow Jones Industrial Average hurdled the 8,000 barrier to close up 63.17 points at 8,038.88.
London's FTSE index of blue chips followed suit in early trade on Thursday and flirted with the 5,000 level. By early afternoon it was off 18.3 points at 4,945.9.
The buoyant mood also helped propel the 30-year Treasury bond yield below 6.5 percent. The long bond was trading at 101-27 in London, yielding 6.48 percent.
"If we can see this 30-year hold below 6.5 percent by the end of this week, then I think that's going to provide the door to another good rally coming through," said Hawkins.
"At this stage it looks as if we can see additional gains coming through in both stocks and bonds."
But some economists say that with investors on tenterhooks for the next interest rate rise in the U.S., crunch time is approaching.

"We are still in a disinflationary environment and it's not just a symptom of cyclical factors -- it does reflect a lot of structural changes," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International in London.
"But we are at a very interesting phase of this disinflationary story -- the U.S. and UK are at an advanced stage of the cycle."
He said there was a risk of rising inflation in those economies but he did not expect it to happen.
"It would require a strong global economic recovery leading to relaxed policy stances for a pickup in general inflation -- but that's very unlikely to occur," said Lyons.
Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking, was slightly less sanguine.

"It's still possible for governments and central banks to generate inflation in these conditions if they make policy errors," he said. "And the trouble is, governments only know they've made them after the events."
Lewis said the low yields in government bond markets would last as long as the low inflation lasted.
"But if the Fed really is being too expansive at the moment, and is not taking account of the inflation risks, we will see yields going up in one or two years' time."
For asset markets the good times are still rolling but dealers know they will have to end some time.
"Markets are going to rise, rise, rise until there is no single short left -- and then it's going to fall apart," said Charles Quigley, vice-president at Chase in London.
